meaning: Fomorian king whose destructive eye blasts armies when its lid is raised, slain by his grandson Lúg with a sling-stone at Cath Maige Tuired.

phonemes.desc: Voiced bilabial stop [b], broad (velarized) before a; as in English 'bay' but with the back of the tongue raised.
Short open [a], the stressed vowel of the first syllable — the 'ah' of 'father' held brief.
Broad (velarized) lateral [l̪ˠ], the dark Irish l with the tongue toward the teeth and the back raised — never the light l of English 'leaf'.
Short [o] closing on a broad trilled or tapped r [rˠ]; the second syllable unstressed, as in all Old Irish words stressed on the first.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BAH-lor' — stress the first syllable hard, keep the l dark and broad, and let the final r stay tapped. Modern Irish 'Balor' keeps essentially the same shape.

pronunciation.note: Balor is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Irish form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the Fomorian king's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: The King of the Evil Eye
domains.subtitle: The Venomed Gaze, the Fomorian Tribute, the Fortress of Tory, the Grandson's Stone
domains.lead: Balor — Balor Béimnech, 'Balor of the Mighty Blows' — is king of the Fomorians, the sea-borne oppressors of medieval Irish tradition, and owner of the most feared weapon in the whole corpus: a single eye so venomed by the fumes of a druids' brew that no army could stand before its gaze. Grandfather of Lugh and doomed by that very grandson's sling-stone at Mag Tuired, he is the Irish tradition's great figure of destructive sovereignty — power that poisons its possessor and is answered, in the end, by his own blood.

cards.name: The Venomed Eye
cards.desc: One eye, poisoned in boyhood by the fumes of a druids' charm-brew; any army it looked upon was worthless, though it were many thousands strong.

cards.name: The Fomorian Tribute
cards.desc: Under Balor and Indech the Fomorians taxed Ireland from the sea, and set the very gods to serf-work until Mag Tuired broke the yoke.

cards.name: The Tower of Tory
cards.desc: In the Donegal oral tradition, the sea-girt tower where Balor prisoned his daughter Eithne against the prophecy of a grandson's hand.

cards.name: The Grandson's Stone
cards.desc: Lugh's sling-stone at Mag Tuired drove the eye backward through Balor's head, so that its own gaze blasted the Fomorian host.

symbols.name: The venomed eye
symbols.meaning: A weapon the owner cannot aim without an army to raise the lid — power that outgrew its possessor

symbols.name: The polished lid-lifter
symbols.meaning: Four men with a handle passed through the eyelid — kingship reduced to machinery, a gaze other men must operate

symbols.name: The tower of Tory
symbols.meaning: The sea-girt prison built against a prophecy — the fortress that made the doom it feared

symbols.name: The Glas Gaibhnenn
symbols.meaning: The grey-green cow Balor stole from Cian in the oral tradition — the theft that set the grandson's birth in motion

symbols.name: The sling-stone
symbols.meaning: The small, aimed answer to the vast, unaimed gaze — the grandson's hand the druids foretold

mythology.lead: Balor's dossier is short and total: he exists in the tradition to be the thing that must be brought down. Cath Maige Tuired gives him the war's most famous single stroke, the Lebor Gabála fixes his lineage and his wife's revenge, and the Donegal oral tradition supplies the prophecy, the tower, and the stolen cow that medieval manuscripts only glance at.

myths.title: Balor Son of Dot, Grandson of Nét
myths.text:
The book of invasions fixes Balor's place before it tells his deeds: Balor mac Doit meic Néit, 'Balor son of Dot, grandson of Nét', king of the Fomorians — the sea-going race who had pressed on Ireland since the age of the Nemedians, exacting tribute from the outer islands. His wife was Cethlenn of the crooked teeth, and it was her spear, or the wound she dealt at Mag Tuired, that killed the Dagda at the Brug years later — the Lebor Gabála records the All-Father's death from Cethlenn's blow as the long-settled price of Balor's war.

His daughter was Ethniu, and she was given to Cian, son of Dian Cécht the healer; their son was Lugh, the Samildánach, equally skilled in all arts. Thus the Fomorian king was the grandfather of the Túatha Dé Danann's deliverer — the genealogy that the whole tragedy of Mag Tuired turns on.

myths.title: How the Eye Was Poisoned
myths.text:
Cath Maige Tuired explains the weapon before it uses it. Balor had a destructive eye, never opened except on a battlefield, and four men were needed to raise its lid with a polished handle that passed through it. Any army that eye looked upon was made worthless, though it were many thousands strong.

The poison had a childhood. When Balor was a boy, his father's druids were brewing a charm, and the boy looked in on the work; the fumes of the brew rose and struck the eye, and from that day its gaze was venom. The detail is the tradition's whole theory of the figure in one image: power taken in unguarded, as a child takes in smoke, and carried incurably for a lifetime.

myths.title: The Tower and the Prophecy
myths.text:
The medieval manuscripts know that Ethniu was Balor's daughter and Lugh's mother; how that came to be is told by the oral tradition of the north-west, collected in the nineteenth century on and around Tory Island — Balor's sea-girt fortress off the Donegal coast. A druid foretold that Balor would die by the hand of his own grandson, and the king answered the prophecy with masonry: he locked his daughter Eithne in a tower on the rock, with twelve matrons to keep every man from her sight.

The doom came in by the usual door. Balor coveted the Glas Gaibhnenn, the grey-green cow of Cian, and stole her across the water; Cian crossed to Tory for redress, and with the help of the druidess Biróg won into the tower in woman's dress and to Eithne's side. When the child was born Balor had him cast into the sea — but the sea gave him back, fostered and hidden, until a young stranger called Lugh came to Nuadu's court at Tara and was asked what art he practiced. The question the Fomorians could not answer had been growing up under their own doom all along.

myths.title: The Sling-Stone at Mag Tuired
myths.text:
At the second battle of Mag Tuired the armies broke each other all day, and then Balor came against the Túatha Dé Danann with the Fomorian host, destroying and slaughtering. He commanded that the lid of his eye be raised, so that he might blast the enemy with its look — and the four men set the polished handle to the lid.

It was then that Lugh cast a sling-stone at him, which carried the eye backward through his head, so that it was his own host that looked into it. Balor fell on top of the Fomorian fighting-men, and twenty-seven of them died beneath his side. The weapon the Fomorians had built their tyranny on spent its last gaze on its owners — and the battle turned with the eye. Afterward the Túatha Dé Danann took the tribute back from the defeated host, and the power of the Fomorians over Ireland was broken for good.

lore.syncretism: Balor's clearest cross-border witnesses are comparative, not cognate. The Welsh corpus preserves no figure derived from the same name — the Brythonic silence is total, as it is for so many of the Fomorian cycle. The parallels the scholarship actually leans on are typological. First, the Greek Acrisius: the king who prisoned his daughter Danae in a bronze chamber because a prophecy named her son his slayer, and died by that grandson Perseus all the same — the Eithne tower is the same tale-shape, and comparatists have set the two side by side since the nineteenth century. Second, the one-eyed monster answered by aimed cunning — the Polyphemus pattern — where the single enormous eye is both the ogre's strength and the one place he can be struck. Third, and nearest home, the Irish and Mediterranean complex of the evil eye itself: the belief that a look can wither cattle, milk, and men, which Sjoestedt and Mac Cana both treat as the living folk-ground of Balor's venomed gaze. O'Rahilly read him further, as a figure of death and the western sea; the handbooks register the reading without making it doctrine.
lore.culturalLegacy: Balor entered the modern world through two doors. The first was scholarship: Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) carried the sling-stone and the tower into English reading, and O'Rahilly's Early Irish History and Mythology (1946) made him the type-case of the Irish death-king, a scholarly afterlife as large as his medieval dossier is short. The second was the folklore itself: the Donegal oral versions — the tower, the stolen cow, the child cast into the sea — were collected in the nineteenth century and never stopped being retold, and 'Balor of the Evil Eye' remains the standing name of the figure in Irish and in English. In the modern imagination he has become the Celtic dark lord par excellence: the remote tyrant in his island fortress whose one weapon poisons everything it touches, answered not by a greater weapon but by the prophesied grandchild the fortress was built to prevent. Tory Island keeps his address; the Irish language never lost his name.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Every part of Balor's story is about containment failing. The eye is contained — cloaked, lidded, lifted only by machinery — and containment is the whole catastrophe: a gaze so dangerous it must be operated by four other men is no longer a weapon but an occupation, a king reduced to the caretaker of his own poison. The daughter is contained in a tower against a prophecy, and the tower is the prophecy's instrument: no tower, no Cian, no Lugh. Balor is the tradition's purest study of power that can only destroy — he is given no craft, no counsel, no feast, no children worth the having, nothing but the eye and the tax it enforces.

And the answer the tradition gives him is exact. Not a bigger eye, not a stronger king, but a sling-stone: small, aimed, and thrown by the one hand the whole machinery existed to forestall. The venom that could wither an army is turned in a single instant into the Fomorians' own epitaph — it was his own host that looked into it. That is the Irish judgment on the evil eye, and on every power built to wither rather than to make: it ends by looking inward. The grandson does not defeat the weapon. He simply turns it around.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Balor — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: balor.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Balor is a textual and oral figure: no ogham stone names him, no votive inscription invokes him, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. His manuscript witnesses are exact — Cath Maige Tuired survives uniquely in the sixteenth-century British Library MS Harley 5280, the basis of Gray's edition, while Lebor Gabála Érenn is preserved in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster and its sister codices. His geographical anchor is one of the most dramatic pieces of coastline in Europe: Tory Island (Toraigh), nine miles off the Bloody Foreland of Donegal, whose cliffs and sea-stacks — above all the great rock called Tór Mór — the oral tradition names as Balor's fortress and the site of Eithne's tower. The nineteenth-century collectors who wrote the tower story down were recording a living Donegal tradition anchored to those rocks, and the island's medieval monastic remains and round tower have kept the name in continuous local memory.
